prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores how love, art, value, and identity are measured across earthly, infernal, and paradisiacal realms through surreal comparison, literary allusion, and absurdist self-address. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Love, That

outputs.L1:
The unit of wine is the cup. Of love, the unit is the kiss. That is here.  
In Hell, the units are the gallon and the fuck. In Paradise, the drop and the glance.  

Ants are my heroes. They debate, and they obey. They can sit at a table for eight hours, drawing.  
They identify the under-theorized . . .  

Have some, for they are as abundant here as flecks of mica in the Iowa night sky.  

What are twenty-sided dishes of fancy almonds? What use are jewels?  
He is Kālidāsa. You are nothing. Or rather, you are a tray of stainless-steel cones.  

Meanwhile, one opens *Kumārasambhava* to find rainbow-colored crystals pointing every which way.  

Nice try. You are a tank-builder, yet you refuse to build tanks.  
And so now you are to be watched over by three heckling birds, evilly named, discomfiting to children.  

¡Fíjate! You are to be watched by three fowl, commonplace in Florida. Even these three hearty objectionables:  
the blue tit, the woodpecker, and the swampcunt.  

I am one to talk. I am so twisted up that my only hope is Salena, my physical therapist,  
with the eyes of Athena and the hands of a destroying eagle.
outputs.L2:
Wine is measured by cups; Love is measured by kisses. That is how it works in this place.  
In Hell, the measures become gallons and sex. In Paradise, they shrink to droplets and looks.

Ants are the figures I admire. They argue, then comply. They are capable of spending eight hours seated at a table, making drawings. They notice what has not been theorized enough . . .  
Take some, since around here they are plentiful, like specks of mica scattered across an Iowa night sky.

What purpose do ornate twenty-sided almond plates serve? What good are gems?  
He is Kālidāsa. You amount to nothing. More precisely, you are a serving tray covered with stainless-steel cones.

At the same time, someone opens the Kumārasambhava and finds multicolored crystals aimed in every direction.  
Good effort. You design tanks, yet you will not make tanks. Therefore, from now on, you must be supervised by three jeering birds with wicked names, unsettling to children.

Look! Your guardians are to be three ordinary Florida birds. These three robustly disagreeable ones: the blue tit, the woodpecker, and the swampcunt.

Not that I’m in any position to judge. I am so contorted that my sole chance is Salena, my physical therapist, whose eyes are like Athena’s and whose hands resemble those of a ravaging eagle.
outputs.L3:
The text contrasts different measures of experience—earthly, hellish, and paradisiacal—through vivid images of quantity and intensity. Ordinary life is associated with familiar units such as cups and kisses, while suffering is imagined in harsher, excessive terms, like gallons. Paradise, by contrast, is suggested through the smallest and most delicate measures: drops and glances. These images create a scale of experience in which value is not always tied to abundance. A single glance or drop may carry more meaning than a vast quantity of something painful or ordinary.

The text also praises ants as heroic figures. They are admired not simply for their labor, but for the combination of qualities they represent. Ants debate, obey, endure, and remain attentive to tiny details that others ignore. Their heroism lies in their collective discipline and their capacity to notice what is overlooked. By elevating ants in this way, the speaker challenges conventional ideas of greatness and suggests that true nobility may be found in persistence, cooperation, and attention.

At the same time, the speaker dismisses material luxury and personal importance. Jewels, refined possessions, and fancy objects are treated as insignificant when placed beside the greatness of Kālidāsa. This contrast reduces worldly status and ornament to triviality. The speaker implies that artistic and spiritual greatness far exceed material splendor, and that the self should not be inflated by wealth, taste, or social importance.

The addressee is portrayed as someone with the ability to create something useful and sustaining, especially through the image of building tanks. Yet this person refuses or fails to act on that capacity. As a result, they are watched by three hostile birds, figures that suggest judgment, threat, or accusation. The image implies that neglected responsibility invites scrutiny and that unused power becomes a source of moral tension.

The text ends by turning inward. After criticizing others and weighing different forms of greatness and failure, the speaker offers self-criticism as well. This closing movement softens the earlier judgments and reveals a desire for healing. That hope is associated with Salena, a physical therapist described in almost divine terms, with sacred eyes and fierce hands. She represents both compassion and severity: someone who can see deeply, touch painfully, and restore the damaged body. Through her, the text concludes with the possibility that pain, discipline, and care may lead toward recovery.
outputs.L4:
Across earthly, infernal, and paradisiacal realms, the text asks how anything can be measured: love, art, value, identity, suffering, obedience, hunger, and the self. Its comparisons are surreal because ordinary scales have failed. A human life cannot be weighed like metal, a poem cannot be priced like bread, and love cannot be calculated by distance, duration, or usefulness. Yet the speaker keeps trying to compare unlike things, as if the only way to approach truth is through impossible equivalence. Heaven, hell, and earth become not stable locations but experimental chambers in which different systems of value are tested and found inadequate.

In the earthly realm, measurement appears practical at first. Things are judged by what they do, what they cost, whom they serve, and how visibly they endure. A body is understood through appetite, labor, fatigue, and desire. Art is judged by its beauty or usefulness; love is judged by loyalty, sacrifice, or proof. But these measures quickly become absurd. Usefulness begins to look like a form of servitude. Grandeur begins to look theatrical, inflated, or empty. A magnificent object may be no more meaningful than a small gesture; a heroic declaration may matter less than the private recognition of another person’s pain. Earthly value is therefore unstable, because the world insists on counting what cannot truly be counted.

The infernal realm intensifies this instability. Hell is not merely a place of punishment but a place where measurement becomes grotesque. Everything is exaggerated, distorted, and made literal. Obedience becomes monstrous; refusal becomes both dignity and damnation. The body is reduced to need, yet that need speaks with disturbing honesty. Hunger, pain, and desire strip away the decorative language of virtue. In this infernal atmosphere, the self confronts its own humiliations and contradictions. It may wish to be noble, but it must also eat; it may wish to be free, but it is shaped by commands; it may wish to transcend the flesh, but the flesh remains the first and last instrument of perception.

The paradisiacal realm does not simply solve these problems. Paradise, too, has its strange measures. It promises perfection, harmony, and final meaning, but perfection can become another kind of abstraction. If everything is complete, then longing disappears; if all value is fixed, then perception no longer has to struggle. The text seems suspicious of any realm that offers too clean an answer. Paradise may illuminate, but it may also flatten. It may redeem earthly confusion, but it may also erase the intimate, awkward, bodily forms through which meaning is actually discovered. Even transcendence must be questioned if it demands the abandonment of particularity.

Through literary allusion, the text places itself in conversation with inherited systems of meaning. Echoes of sacred journeys, epic descents, mystical visions, and philosophical arguments hover behind its images. These allusions suggest that the speaker is not alone in attempting to map love and value across cosmic dimensions. Earlier writers also imagined the soul moving through ordered realms, learning how sin, virtue, beauty, and truth might be ranked. But here those old hierarchies are unsettled. The grand architecture of heaven, hell, and earth remains, yet it is filled with absurd, intimate, and unstable images. Tradition provides a structure, but the speaker refuses to let that structure become final.

The absurdist self-address sharpens this refusal. The speaker turns upon itself, questions itself, mocks itself, and treats its own identity as something provisional. The “I” is not a secure unit of meaning. It is a voice trying to measure itself while knowing that the measuring instrument is damaged. This self-address can be comic, desperate, tender, or accusatory. It exposes the gap between what the self wants to be and what it actually is. The speaker may aspire to grandeur, but it encounters need; it may seek revelation, but it stumbles into ridiculous comparison; it may long for divine order, but it remains trapped in the strange theater of its own perceptions.

As a result, grandeur and usefulness collapse into shifting images. The great may become small, the small may become immense, and the useful may become spiritually empty. Obedience, which might once have seemed virtuous, appears ambiguous: it can be devotion, cowardice, discipline, or surrender. Refusal, likewise, is unstable: it can be rebellion, pride, integrity, or despair. Bodily need interrupts both categories. A hungry body does not care for metaphysical rank; a desiring body does not fit neatly into moral geometry. The body insists that meaning is not made only in the mind or the soul, but also in sensation, vulnerability, and dependence.

The text ultimately suggests that meaning survives not through fixed units of measurement but through acts of perception. To perceive strangely is not to perceive falsely. On the contrary, the surreal image may come closer to truth than a rational scale, because it preserves contradiction. Love may be absurd and sacred at once. Art may be useless and necessary. The self may be comic and tragic, obedient and rebellious, earthly and otherworldly. Meaning endures in the ability to notice these tensions without resolving them too quickly.

What remains, then, is not a stable hierarchy but an intimate practice of attention. The speaker measures by looking, comparing, misrecognizing, correcting, and looking again. The world is not made meaningful because it can be organized into perfect categories. It is meaningful because perception continues even after categories fail. In the strange space between heaven, hell, and earth, the text discovers a fragile but persistent form of value: not value as price, rank, or utility, but value as the charged encounter between a mind, a body, and the images through which they attempt to understand themselves.
outputs.L5:
**The Love That Remains**

The love that truly matters is not always loud or dramatic. Sometimes, it is quiet. It is found in small acts of kindness, in patient understanding, and in the comfort of knowing someone is there even when words are not enough.

The love that stays through difficult times is the love that teaches us strength. It does not disappear when life becomes complicated. Instead, it grows deeper, becoming a source of hope and courage.

The love that changes us is the love that helps us become better people. It reminds us to forgive, to listen, and to care not only for others but also for ourselves.

In the end, the love that lasts is not measured by perfect moments, but by loyalty, trust, and the willingness to keep choosing one another every day.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in the style of contemporary experimental poetry, mixing classical Indian references, odd units of measurement, ants, Iowa night skies, heckling birds, Spanish interjections, and a physical therapist named Salena.
counterfactuals.output:
Salena measures my grief in cubits of moonmilk,  
in furlongs of fascia, in one-eighth teaspoon of thunder  
under the left scapula.

“Breathe,” she says, and the room becomes Iowa—  
black cornfields stitched to a sky so wide  
it could be Vyasa’s unwritten appendix,  
all those stars muttering their Sanskrit homework.

Ants cross the treatment table in a disciplined empire,  
each carrying a sesame seed, a verdict, a tiny conch shell.  
They are headed toward Kurukshetra or maybe Des Moines.  
The difference tonight is measured in barn-owls per acre.

From the gutter, the grackles heckle my enlightenment.  
“Nice posture, Arjuna!” they shriek.  
“Try warrior pose without the war!”  
Ay, dios mío, say the crickets, sawing the dark into usable inches.

Salena presses a thumb into the knot  
where my previous lives have pooled.  
Out spills Ganga water, insurance paperwork,  
a blue plastic bead from some childhood I deny owning.

The ceiling fan turns like a tired chakra.  
The ants applaud with their infinitesimal wrists.  
Somewhere above Iowa, Indra misplaces his raincloud  
and borrows a combine instead.

“Pain is information,” Salena says,  
and the sentence opens like a lotus in a strip mall fountain.  
No, no, claro que no—  
pain is a parrot wearing a judge’s wig,  
a mile-long invoice,  
a crow with a tiny megaphone yelling,  
“Objection! Objection!”

By midnight my spine is realigned  
to the exact latitude of a cow dreaming in Vedic meter.  
The stars lean lower, curious and rude.  
The birds refuse to let anyone be holy in peace.

I walk home carrying my body  
like a brass lamp through soybean vapor,  
while the ants, those black commas of the underworld,  
rewrite the road beneath me:

not salvation,  
not diagnosis,  
but a small door of sugar  
opening and opening  
inside the enormous dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a strange, fragmented poem that begins “The unit of wine is the cup. Of Love, the unit is the kiss,” and then spirals into absurd images involving Hell, Paradise, ants, Kālidāsa, tank-builders, Florida birds, and Athena.
counterfactuals.output:
The unit of wine is the cup. Of Love, the unit is the kiss,  
but Hell measures itself in teaspoons of smoke,  
in receipts burned before purchase,  
in the left shoe of a pilgrim  
filled with rain.

Paradise—  
a green bureaucracy of wings.  
Every angel stamped twice,  
every harp inspected for ants.

Ants in the sugar bowl,  
ants in the crown of the king,  
ants carrying away the vowels  
from Kālidāsa’s moonlit cloud—  
O messenger, wait:  
your sky has been requisitioned  
by tank-builders.

They arrive with blueprints for thunder.  
They rivet the horizon.  
They pour concrete into the lotus.  
They name each cannon after a flower  
and each flower after a debt.

Florida birds stand in the mangroves,  
pink and judicial,  
balancing on one leg  
like punctuation marks  
that have lost their sentences.

A pelican opens its bill:  
inside, a courtroom,  
inside that, a desert,  
inside that, Athena  
polishing an owl’s small helmet.

“Wisdom,” she says,  
“is mostly feathers and refusal.”

Meanwhile Hell is renting bicycles.  
Paradise is out of stamps.  
The ants have translated everything  
into crumbs.

Kālidāsa laughs from behind a monsoon,  
his sandals full of stars,  
his inkpot full of mosquitoes.  
The tank-builders ask him  
for a permit to dream.

No.

The cup breaks.  
The kiss evaporates.  
Athena plants an olive tree  
in the mouth of a machine.

And the Florida birds—  
those improbable officials of dawn—  
sign the sky  
with their long, bewildered legs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an avant-garde literary collage with abrupt tonal shifts, mythological allusions, vulgar humor, and non sequiturs; include Kumārasambhava, fancy almonds, stainless steel cones, three malicious birds, and a final line about a physical therapist.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn, the mountain put on its widow’s veil and called it weather.

In the footnote to a scream, **Kumārasambhava** bloomed like a saffron bruise: Pārvatī counting her ribs as prayer beads, Śiva pretending not to notice the universe licking ash from his shoulder. The gods, management consultants in golden sandals, convened to discuss desire, quarterly losses, and the unacceptable productivity of demons.

Then someone brought out the **fancy almonds**.

They were sugared, aristocratic, each one wearing a tiny powdered wig. I ate seven and immediately understood French dentistry, the sorrow of chandeliers, and why kings always look like they need to fart but can’t because of etiquette.

CUT TO: a warehouse of **stainless steel cones**.

They gleamed with the sterile ambition of failed rockets. A man named Trevor stacked them according to no known cosmology. “These,” he whispered, “are for catching the voices of extinct accountants.” Behind him, a radio coughed up a polka, then a weather report, then my grandmother saying, “Never trust a soup with a zipper.”

Enter: **three malicious birds**.

One was a crow with a lawyer’s briefcase.  
One was a peacock with knives for eyelashes.  
One was a pigeon named Sir Bastard who had learned the flute only to ruin funerals.

They circled the moon, heckling it.

“Nice craters, idiot!” shrieked the peacock.

The crow filed an injunction against tenderness.

The pigeon shat on a statue of Apollo and called it literary criticism.

Meanwhile, in the basement of time, a centaur tried online dating. His profile read: HALF HORSE, HALF REGRET, FULLY VACCINATED. No matches, except a cyclops who only sent blurry photos of omelets.

O Muse, lend me your stapler.

I wish to fasten together: a tax receipt, a lock of blue hair, the smell of burnt toast, the Bhagavad Gītā in a motel drawer, one obscene limerick about Zeus and a patio umbrella, and the trembling invoice for my own reincarnation.

The sea applauded incorrectly.

Somewhere a baby laughed with the voice of a corrupt senator. Somewhere else, a saint removed his halo and used it as a frisbee. The sky developed a rash shaped like Belgium. All philosophy was briefly replaced by mayonnaise.

And love?

Love arrived late, drunk, wearing one boot and carrying a bag of oranges it insisted were “emotional support grenades.” It kissed the wrong person, apologized to a lamppost, and vomited behind the temple of Sarasvatī.

Still, the cosmos continued chewing.

Still, the almonds glittered in their ridiculous bowl.

Still, the stainless steel cones waited for revelation, or soup.

Still, the three malicious birds rehearsed a barbershop quartet called *The Beak Apocalypse*.

I turned the page and found no page, only a tendon, warm and instructive.

The final prophecy was delivered by a physical therapist.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a bizarre poetic monologue that sounds like a hallucinated translation of a highbrow modernist poem—include measurements of love and hell, ants as intellectual heroes, jewels, Kālidāsa, Spanish slang, and grotesquely named birds.
counterfactuals.output:
I measured love in teaspoons of lightning,  
in cubits of insomnia, in the small blue meters  
between your shoulder and my catastrophe.  
Hell, meanwhile, was calibrated in bureaucratic miles:  
three forms per shriek, seven stamps per furnace,  
a corridor of velvet ash where the clocks wore lipstick  
and asked, *¿qué onda, mi cielo roto?*

O jewels! O little tyrannies of light!  
Rubies like coagulated applause, emeralds  
with the green boredom of old professors,  
sapphires coughing up the sea in fragments—  
I put them on my tongue and pronounced Kālidāsa  
backwards, and the clouds immediately became legal witnesses.  
Even the moon, that dandified coconut,  
leaned over the balcony and said: *órale, qué tragedia más fina.*

But the ants—ah, the ants!—  
they were the true intellectual heroes.  
Each carried a crumb of Plato through the sugar ruins,  
each antenna trembled with dialectical thunder.  
One ant, Professor Mandíbula, disproved the soul  
by dragging a dead wasp across a chessboard.  
Another translated rain into footnotes.  
A third founded a tiny academy inside my sleeve  
and lectured all night on the metaphysics of jam.

Do not ask me where the birds came from.  
They arrived already named, horribly, nobly:  
the Mucus-Crowned Trumpet-Screecher,  
the Velvet Gizzard Cardinal,  
the Bonebeak of Saint Regret,  
the Grand Putrescent Lark,  
and that most tender of monsters,  
the Little Pink Throat-Wound Finch.  
They perched in the chandelier like guilty verbs,  
singing arias of spoiled milk and imperial weather.

Beloved, I tell you plainly:  
your absence weighs nine kilograms of violet fire.  
Your kiss is a province measured in broken mirrors.  
My despair is two hectares of boiling lace.  
I have converted longing into hectares,  
hell into teaspoons,  
and my heart into a municipal fountain  
where drunks wash their crowns and mutter,  
*no manches, la eternidad está cruda.*

Kālidāsa walks beside me in a coat of monsoon silk,  
holding a jewel the size of a murdered planet.  
He says the seasons are merely the disguises of desire.  
He says a cloud can be a messenger  
if you injure it beautifully enough.  
He says the ants know everything  
but will reveal it only to sugar, corpses, and children.

So I lie down in the garden of incorrect translations.  
The flowers all have the faces of minor diplomats.  
The grass recites obsolete laws.  
The grotesque birds peck at the hinges of dawn,  
and somewhere beneath the marble,  
beneath the opera of worms,  
the ants continue their heroic seminar—  
tiny dark scholars marching  
through the jeweled intestines of the world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, absurdist poem with surreal metaphors and academic-sounding phrasing, blending paradise/hell imagery, insects, Sanskrit literature, Iowa, Florida wildlife, profanity, and a closing invocation of Salena the physical therapist.
counterfactuals.output:
In the peach-lit vestibule between paradise and the DMV,  
where hell wears a hibiscus behind its ear  
and lectures on comparative eschatology to a room of wet mosquitoes,  
Iowa rises like a corn-fed mandala from the blackboard—  
all silos, thunderheads, and metaphysical hogs  
reciting the *Ṛg Veda* through their teeth.

O Florida, swamp-gospel appendix of Eden,  
your alligators lounge like tenured demons in chlorophyll robes,  
your ibises pick footnotes from the skulls of tourists,  
your palmetto bugs—those glossy little professors of dread—  
skitter across the kitchen of being  
with the confidence of minor gods and total bastards.

Somewhere, Kālidāsa is drunk in a Winn-Dixie parking lot,  
comparing cloud-messengers to vape smoke,  
while Sītā, incandescent as a motel vacancy sign,  
argues with a cicada about exile, humidity, and the ethics  
of turning grief into ornamental Sanskrit.  
The cicada says: *fuck the kingdom*,  
and dissolves into applause.

Behold the infernal orange grove:  
each fruit a blistering sun, each blossom a subpoena,  
each bee a gold-plated monk buzzing *neti neti*  
above the drainage ditch where paradise leaks antifreeze.  
In Des Moines, meanwhile, snow falls upward  
like shredded scripture returning to the mouth of God,  
and every grain elevator becomes a crooked steeple  
for worshippers of the sacred, the stupid, the annihilatingly beige.

I have seen dragonflies stitch heaven to a septic tank.  
I have seen cockroaches crowned with jasmine  
drag the chariot of Arjuna through a Publix deli.  
I have seen the moon—huge, bruised, bureaucratic—  
stamp my soul “provisionally redeemed”  
and toss it to the sandhill cranes,  
those prehistoric lawyers of the marsh.

Therefore let us formulate a thesis:  
that bliss is a flamingo standing on one leg in Gehenna;  
that damnation is a faculty meeting held inside a mango;  
that the body, poor magnificent asshole,  
is merely a wet dissertation defended before insects  
in a language older than thunder.

And when the spine becomes a serpent-commentary,  
when the knees file appeals in the court of karma,  
when the shoulder sings like a conch full of gravel—  
come then, with cool hands and practical mercy,  
O Salena the physical therapist,  
patroness of tendons, corrector of doomed posture,  
stretch us from hell toward paradise,  
and release the locusts from our lower backs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
